result:
The proposed answer of 3/8 is wrong. The limit should be 1/3, as the check below shows.

**Where the argument breaks.** The solution treats the cells of C (the odd-odd cells) as removable, as long as the vertex-cover condition holds. That ignores the requirement that hole boundaries be disjoint from the outer boundary and from each other.

**The corner cells of a hole must be in P.** Take a single-cell hole at (0,0). Its corner vertex (1,1) belongs to the diagonal cell (1,1).

- If cell (1,1) is empty, it is part of the complement of P. Its boundary then passes through the corner vertex of the hole.
- That empty cell lies either in the outer region or in another hole. Either way, a hole boundary meets another boundary component at that vertex, which is forbidden.

So all 8 neighbours of every single-cell hole must lie in P. This forces every C cell next to a hole to be filled, so the savings from deleting C cells in the proposed construction are not allowed.

**Upper bound for single-cell holes.** Every hole cell has all 8 of its neighbours in P, so two holes cannot be king-adjacent. Hence holes have density at most 1/4 in the plane. The non-hole cells have density at least 3/4, and all of them are in P in the densest arrangement. That gives at least 3 cells of P per hole, so h ≤ n/3 asymptotically.

**Construction.** Place holes on the lattice (2i, 2j) and fill every other cell in the region. This uses 3 cells of P per hole and gives h/n → 1/3.

**Larger holes.** I did not prove that larger holes cannot beat single-cell holes. They should be less efficient, since each hole still needs a full surrounding ring in P. The 3/8 claim already fails on the single-cell bound, and I take 1/3 to be the true limit.

The proposed answer 3/8 exceeds this bound, so it is incorrect.

VERDICT: REJECT
